People's Republic of Bulgaria: Bulgarian. Bulgaria was also part of Comecon as well as a member of the Warsaw Pact.

Batavian Republic: Dutch. The Batavian Republic was the successor state to the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands.

Founder of the Junbish-e Milli party and a veteran of the Soviet-Afghan War, this Afghan warlord sided with the winning side so consistently he earned the nickname 'kingmaker' — who is he?
Abdul Rashid Dostum (born 1954) is an Afghan exiled politician, former military officer and warlord.
This Italian statesman served five terms as prime minister and pursued a pro-Arab foreign policy before being kidnapped by the Red Brigades in March 1978 — who was he?
Aldo Moro (23 September 1916 - 9 May 1978) was an Italian statesman and prominent member of Christian Democracy (DC) and its centre-left wing.
Described as Volodymyr Zelenskyy's right-hand man and dubbed Kyiv's 'Green Cardinal' by Politico, this former film producer headed the Ukrainian president's office from 2020 to 2025. Who is he?
Andriy Yermak (born 21 November 1971) is a Ukrainian politician and former film producer who served as the head of the Office of the President of Ukraine from 2020 to 2025.
Known by the nickname Kráka, this woman of Norse legend is remembered in the sagas as one of Ragnar Lodbrok's wives — who is she?
Aslaug (Old), also called Aslg, Krka or Kraba, is a figure in Norse mythology who appears in Snorri's Edda, the Vlsunga saga and in the saga of Ragnar Lodbrok as one of his wives.
Known colloquially as PNoy, this 15th president of the Philippines was the son of an assassinated senator and the 11th president — who was he?
Benigno Aquino III (locally; February 8, 1960 - June 24, 2021), also known colloquially as PNoy, was the 15th president of the Philippines, serving from 2010 to 2016.
Installed as high priest by the Roman procurator Valerius Gratus, this New Testament figure is described as the organizer behind Jesus's trial before the Sanhedrin — who was he?
Caiaphas was a High Priest of Israel during the first century.

This monarch's court physician, Johann Friedrich Struensee, effectively ran Denmark and Norway for two years before being overthrown in an 1772 coup, after which the ruler's own son eventually acted as unofficial regent — who was he?
Christian VII (29 January 1749 - 13 March 1808) was King of Denmark and Norway and Duke of Schleswig and Holstein from 1766 until his death in 1808.
This American anthropologist and anarchist gave the Occupy movement a leading voice and wrote provocative books like Debt: The First 5,000 Years and Bullshit Jobs — who was he?
David Graeber (February 12, 1961 - September 2, 2020) was an American anthropologist and anarchist social and political activist.
A grandson of Alfred the Great, this English king took the throne in 939 and died young in a brawl with an outlaw at Pucklechurch — who was he?
Edmund I (920/921 - 26 May 946) was King of the English from 27 October 939 until his death in 946.
A member of the Unity party, this Latvian politician led the government from 2023 until resigning in May 2026, remaining as caretaker until her successor took office two weeks later — who is she?
Evika Siliņa (born 3 August 1975) is a Latvian politician who served as prime minister of Latvia from 2023 to 2026.
The third woman ever elected to Congress from Arizona, this politician left office in 2012 after a severe brain injury from an assassination attempt — who is she?
Gabby Giffords (born June 8, 1970) is an American retired politician and gun violence prevention advocate.
Triggered by the 1929 Wall Street crash, this decade-long global economic downturn brought mass unemployment to the US, UK, and Germany — name the era?
Great Depression was a severe global economic downturn from 1929 to 1939.
In Norse mythology, this female being presides over an underworld realm that shares her name, receiving a portion of the dead — who is she?
Hel (mythological being) (Old Norse) is a female being in Norse mythology who is said to preside over an underworld realm of the same name, where she receives a portion of the dead.
Though scholars generally consider her fictional, which legendary Chinese folk heroine is said to have lived during the Northern and Southern dynasties era?
Hua Mulan (traditional; simplified; pinyin: Hu Mln) is a legendary Chinese folk heroine from the Northern and Southern dynasties era (4th to 6th century AD) of Chinese history.
Co-ruling with his far more famous younger half-brother, later known as 'the Great,' this physically and mentally impaired tsar held a purely titular crown from 1682 to 1696 — who was he?
Ivan V of Russia was Tsar of Russia (1682–1696). Ivan's reign was solely titular because he had serious physical and mental challenges.
A flight lieutenant who seized power in a 1979 coup, this aviator went on to become his country's longest-serving leader across 19 years — who was he?
Jerry Rawlings (22 June 1947 - 12 November 2020) was a Ghanaian military officer, aviator, politician, and revolutionary who led the country briefly in 1979 and then from 1981 to 2001.
Whose son Bernardo became President of Guatemala in 2024, decades after this philosophy-professor-turned-statesman first won the office democratically in 1945?
Juan José Arévalo (10 September 1904 - 8 October 1990) was a Guatemalan statesman and professor of philosophy who became Guatemala's first democratically elected president in 1945.

Splitting from the Kingdom of León in 1065, reuniting with it between 1072 and 1157, and permanently merging after 1230, this medieval Iberian realm led extensive conquests into Islamic-held southern Iberia — which kingdom?
Kingdom of Castile was a polity in the Iberian Peninsula during the Middle Ages.
The 1848 Democratic presidential nominee, this Michigan senator and Army officer became the leading spokesman for 'popular sovereignty' on slavery — which slave-owning statesman is it?
Lewis Cass (October 9, 1782 - June 17, 1866) was a United States Army officer and politician.
This Indian politician and lawyer from Karnataka has served as President of the Indian National Congress since 2022, and as Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha since 2021 — who is he?

Mallikarjun Kharge (born 21 July 1942) is an Indian politician and lawyer from the Indian state of Karnataka serving as the President of the Indian National Congress since 2022 and Leader of the Opposition in Rajya Sabha since 2021.
Elected to a Moscow municipal seat in 2011, this Russian activist and YouTuber later chaired campaigns for opposition figures like Navalny — who is he?
Maxim Katz (born 23 December 1984) is a Russian political opposition figure, urban planning activist, election campaign strategist, and popular YouTuber hosting his own daily political show.
Known from the Mesha Stele, which describes its victory over the son of Israel's King Omri, this ancient Levantine kingdom's capital was Dibon, in what is now southern Jordan. Name the kingdom?
Moab was an ancient Levantine kingdom whose territory is today located in southern Jordan.
A form of fascism built on the myth of a Nordic Aryan master race, this totalitarian ideology was tied to Adolf Hitler and the NSDAP. What is it?
Nazism (NS), is the far-right, ultranationalist, totalitarian ideology associated with Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party (NSDAP).

Flourishing in what is now Veracruz and Tabasco from roughly 1200 to 400 BC, this early Mesoamerican civilization relocated its center from San Lorenzo to La Venta after the former's decline — who were they?
Olmecs were an early major Mesoamerican civilization, flourishing in the modern-day Mexican states of Veracruz and Tabasco from roughly 1200 to 400 BC during Mesoamerica's formative period.
This Pakistani military officer overthrew Nawaz Sharif's government in a 1999 coup and went on to serve as the country's tenth president — who is he?
Pervez Musharraf (11 August 1943 - 5 February 2023) was a Pakistani politician and military officer who served as the tenth president of Pakistan from 2001 to 2008.
One of the wealthiest Canadians of his era, this New Brunswick-born lawyer made his fortune in a Calgary law partnership before serving as Canada's prime minister from 1930 to 1935 — who was he?
R. B. Bennett (July 3, 1870 - June 26, 1947) was a Canadian lawyer, businessman, philanthropist, and politician who served as the 11th prime minister of Canada from 1930 to 1935.
He represented the Victorian seat of Kooyong for over three decades and became the inaugural leader of the Liberal Party of Australia — which long-serving prime minister?
Robert Menzies (20 December 1894 - 15 May 1978) was an Australian politician and lawyer who served as the 12th prime minister of Australia from 1939 to 1941 and from 1949 to 1966.
Describing herself as an ecofeminist, this politician from the Europe Ecology – The Greens party has served in France's National Assembly since 2022 — who is she?
Sandrine Rousseau (French; born 8 March 1972) is a French economist and politician who has represented the 9th constituency of Paris in the National Assembly since 2022.

Fighting for Finland against the Soviet Union in the brutal Winter War, this sniper is believed to have killed more than 500 enemy soldiers, making him the deadliest sniper in recorded history — who was he?

Simo Häyhä (17 December 1905 - 1 April 2002), often referred to by his nickname The White Death, was a Finnish military sniper during the Winter War between Finland and the Soviet Union in World War II.
In Greek myth, this figure was punished in the underworld, made to stand in a pool beneath a fruit tree, with food and water eternally receding whenever he tried to eat or drink. Who was he?

Tantalus (Ancient Greek: Tantalos), also called Atys, was a Greek mythological figure, most famous for his punishment in Tartarus: he was made to stand in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree, with the fruit and water always receding whenever he tried to eat or drink.
This Indian politician, the son of a Tamil Nadu chief minister, served as the state's youngest-ever deputy chief minister before becoming Opposition Leader in 2026. Who is he?
Udhayanidhi Stalin (born 27 November 1977) is an Indian politician and the incumbent Opposition Leader of Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly since May 2026.

An American civil rights activist who led the NAACP from 1929 until 1955, directing a broad program of legal challenges to racial segregation and disfranchisement. He also worked as a journalist, novelist, and essayist. Who was he?

Walter White (activist) (July 1, 1893 - March 21, 1955) was an American civil rights activist who led the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) for a quarter of a century, from 1929 until 1955.
This French politician became the first woman to serve as President of the National Assembly in 2022, and was re-elected to the post after a snap election in 2024 — who is she?
Grand Duchess Maria Vladimirovna of Russia

Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: Umayyad caliph from 685 to 705. Abd al-Malik's final years were marked by a domestically peaceful and prosperous consolidation of power.

Founded in British India in the late 19th century by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, who claimed to be the promised Messiah and Mahdi awaited by Muslims, this messianic movement is centered on his teachings — name the movement?

Ahmadiyya: Islamic messianic movement founded by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad. Adherents of the Ahmadiyya—a term adopted expressly in reference to Muhammad's alternative name Ahmad—are known as Ahmadi Muslims or simply Ahmadis.

Anastasius I Dicorus: Roman emperor from 491 to 518.
Son of Zeus and twin brother of Artemis, this Greek god of prophecy, music, and healing was the patron deity of the Delphic Oracle. Who is he?
Apollo: Ancient Greek god. Apollo is one of the Olympian deities in ancient Greek religion and mythology.
Originally an oral tradition composed over centuries before being written down in the Sasanian era, this is the core scripture corpus of Zoroastrianism — what is it called?
Avesta: Zoroastrian compendium of sacred literature.

Battles of Lexington and Concord: 1775 battle of the American Revolutionary War.

Capetian dynasty: European royal house of Frankish origin.

Charles Taylor (Liberian politician): President of Liberia from 1997 to 2003.
In Greco-Roman geography, this was the name for the Georgian polity of Egrisi on the Black Sea's eastern coast, home to Zan-speaking ancestors of today's Laz and Mingrelians — what was it?

Dana Perino: American conservative political commentator (born 1972)

The sixth person to walk on the Moon spent nine hours in the Fra Mauro Highlands as Apollo 14's Lunar Module Pilot, and later became a noted ufologist — who was he?
Edgar Mitchell: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1930–2016)
A longtime ally of Robert Mugabe, this ZANU-PF politician was dismissed as vice-president before seizing Zimbabwe's presidency in a 2017 coup — who is he?
Emmerson Mnangagwa: President of Zimbabwe since 2017. Mnangagwa was re-elected in the 2023 Zimbabwean general election with 52.6% of the vote.
Founded in 1933 by the son of a former Spanish dictator, this fascist and national syndicalist movement merged with a rival group the following year to form FE de las JONS — which organization?
Falange Española: Spanish political organization. The Falange Española held its first rally in the Teatro de la Comedia in Madrid on October 29, 1933.
Born in Ferrol, Galicia, he became a brigadier general at just 33 after rising through the ranks in Morocco, then led the Nationalists to victory and ruled Spain until 1975 — who was he?
Francisco Franco: Leader of Spain from 1939 to 1975.
Governor of Central Java for a decade before running for Indonesian president in 2024 alongside former Chief Justice Mahfud MD, this left-wing populist finished third — who is he?
In monotheistic faiths this is seen as the incorporeal creator, sustainer, and ruler of the universe — the very thing atheism rejects and agnosticism deems unknowable. What is it?
God: Supreme being in theistic belief systems.

Ruled by a dynasty once known as the House of Austria, this 1516–1700 European empire commanded territory stretching from the Americas to the Philippines and briefly folded in Portugal — what's this historical era called?
Habsburg Spain: Period of Spanish history (1516–1700)

Often depicted holding twin torches and accompanied by dogs, this Greek goddess of crossroads, night, and magic first appears in Hesiod's 'Theogony' and was worshipped in Athens as a protector of the household — who is she?
Hecate: Greek goddess of magic and transitions. The earliest evidence for Hecate's cult comes from Selinunte, in Sicily.

In the United States, this term describes people and cultures connected to Spain and the Spanish language, applying broadly across Spanish-speaking Latin America and even parts of Africa and Asia once ruled by the Spanish Empire — what term?
Hispanic: Spanish-speaking cultures and persons. The term Hispanic (Spanish: hispano) refers to people, cultures, or countries related to Spain, the Spanish language, or Hispanidad broadly.
This Greek personification of sleep, whose Roman counterpart is Somnus, lent his name to a word for a trance-like state and was said by Pausanias to be the Muses' dearest friend — who is he?
Hypnos: Personification of sleep in Greek mythology. In Greek mythology, Hypnos (Ancient Greek: Ὕπνος, 'sleep'), also spelled Hypnus, is the personification of sleep.
Serving as his country's first president from independence in 1991 until his death in 2016, this Central Asian leader won a disputed election with 86 percent of the vote — who is he?
Islam Karimov: Leader of Uzbekistan from 1989 to 2016.
The last Founding Father to reach the White House, this president of the "Era of Good Feelings" issued a famous doctrine warning Europe off the Americas — who was he?
James Monroe: Founding Father, U.S. president from 1817 to 1825.

In 1127 the Jurchen-led Jin army sacked the Northern Song capital and carted off two emperors at once — a captured ruler and his retired father — in a catastrophe the Chinese still call a 'Humiliation.' Which episode was it?
Jingkang incident: Part of the Jin–Song wars (1127)
Born free in Virginia, this merchant emigrated to a young West African colony in 1829 and went on to become the first man of African descent to govern Liberia as its first president — who is it?
Joseph Jenkins Roberts: 1st and 7th president of Liberia (1848–56, 1872–76)

Founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo after his victory in the Genpei War, this feudal military government ruled Japan from 1185 to 1333, surviving two Mongol invasions before its overthrow — what was it called?

Kamakura shogunate: Government of Japan (1192–1333). The Kamakura shogunate (Japanese: 鎌倉幕府, Hepburn: Kamakura bakufu) was the feudal military government of Japan during the Kamakura period from 1185 to 1333.
Born Kim Song Ju in Japanese-ruled Korea, he founded a country in 1948, ruled it until his death, and was posthumously named its 'Eternal President' — who was he?
Kim Il Sung: Leader of North Korea from 1948 to 1994.
Recorded by the 12th-century chronicler Saxo as a Viking shield-maiden and onetime wife of the legendary Ragnar Lodbrok, this warrior may actually be rooted in myths about a Norse deity — who is she?
Lagertha: Legendary Viking shieldmaiden and ruler.

Shaped by liberal ideas and the non-aggression principle, this political philosophy prizes liberty and personal sovereignty above all, holding you may live as you choose so long as you don't force or defraud others — what is it?
Libertarianism: Political philosophy based on liberty. Different categorizations have been used to distinguish these various forms of libertarianism.
A Burma Campaign veteran regarded as the founder of the Bangladesh Armed Forces, he served as commander-in-chief of the Bangladesh Forces in 1971 — who was this four-star general?
M. A. G. Osmani: Bangladeshi military general & revolutionary (1918–1984)

Educated in Moscow and a veteran of several wars, this military officer was the eldest son of the Chinese Communist Party's founding chairman, before he was killed by a U.S. napalm strike in the Korean War. Who was he?
Mao Anying: Chinese military officer and son of Mao Zedong. Mao Anying (Chinese: 毛岸英; pinyin: Máo Ànyīng; 24 October 1922 – 25 November 1950) was a Chinese military officer.
Leading the Kurdistan Democratic Party since 1979, which politician served as President of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq from 2005 to 2017?
Masoud Barzani: President of the Kurdistan Region from 2005 to 2017.

An ethnic Tutsi army officer who'd helped crush a 1965 Hutu coup, he served as the very last Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Burundi before becoming his country's first president — and ruling as military strongman for a decade until his 1976 overthrow. Who was he?
Crowned with the title Shahanshah, or "King of Kings," in 1967, this last monarch of his dynasty was toppled by the Islamic Revolution. Who is he?
Mohammad Reza Pahlavi: Shah of Iran from 1941 to 1979.
Serving as Lebanon's prime minister across three separate terms since 2005, this politician lost his final bid for a fourth term in January 2025 to the ICJ president, 9 votes to 84 — who is he?
Najib Mikati: Prime Minister of Lebanon (born 1955)
From 1965 to 1977 this Ukrainian-born official served as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet — effectively the Soviet head of state. Who was he?
Born in Iran and raised in Germany, this politician co-led the Greens alongside Ricarda Lang and has served as Vice President of the Bundestag since 2025 — who is he?
This Boston silversmith and engraver turned Patriot is best remembered for a 1775 midnight ride warning minutemen that British troops were on the march — who was he?
Paul Revere: American silversmith and military officer (1735–1818)
Ruling from Napata deep in Nubia, this Kushite king founded Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty in the 8th century BC — who was he?
Piye: Ancient Kushite king and pharaoh.

Known as Bilqis in Arabic and Makeda in Ge'ez, this Hebrew Bible figure brought a caravan of lavish gifts to King Solomon and is linked by modern historians to an ancient South Arabian kingdom in Yemen?
Queen of Sheba: Historical figure in the Abrahamic religions.
Widely considered the greatest mountaineer ever, who made the first solo ascent of Everest and was the first to climb all fourteen eight-thousanders without supplemental oxygen?
Reinhold Messner: Italian mountaineer, adventurer and explorer (born 1944)

Born when Octavian rose to power and established the Augustan Principate in 27 BC, its western half fell in 476 AD while its eastern half lived on until Constantinople fell in 1453. What state is this?
Roman Empire: 27 BC–476/1453 AD state and civilization. The Roman Empire was a state that dominated the Mediterranean and much of Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa during the classical period.

In 1982 this child from Manchester, Maine wrote a letter to Soviet leader Yuri Andropov — and got a personal reply inviting her to visit the USSR, making her 'America's Youngest Ambassador' — who was she?
Samantha Smith: American child peace activist (1972–1985)
Nicknamed "the Grim," this Ottoman sultan grew his empire by seventy percent in just eight years, conquering the entire Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt between 1516 and 1517 — who was he?
Selim I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1512 to 1520.
After a 1969 coup, this army commander became Somalia's third president and reconstituted the country as a one-party Marxist-Leninist state — who is he?
Siad Barre: President of Somalia from 1969 to 1991.

Defined by a one-man police state, forced agricultural collectivization, and a sweeping cult of personality, this set of Soviet policies held sway from 1927 until the dictator's death in 1953 — what is it called?
Stalinism: Political and economic policies implemented by Joseph Stalin.
Led by a man who declared himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ, this 1850s Chinese theocratic state waged a 14-year war against the Qing dynasty — what was it?
Taiping Heavenly Kingdom: Theocratic monarchy in China (1851–1864)
A Whig historian famed for his prose, he both wrote a seminal "History of England" and played a major role in shaping India's education policy — who was he?
Thomas Babington Macaulay: British historian and politician (1800–1859)

Serving as the eighth U.S. director of national intelligence starting in 2025, this former Hawaii congresswoman deployed to Iraq with the National Guard and later left the Democrats to become a Republican — who is she?
Tulsi Gabbard: American politician and military officer (born 1981)
Serving as the 18th U.S. ambassador to NATO before rising to Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, this diplomat briefly served as acting deputy secretary of state in 2023 — who is she?
Fought along the Suez Canal from 1967 to 1970 after Arab leaders adopted the 'three no's' policy, this conflict pitted Israel against Egypt, Jordan, and the PLO?
War of Attrition: 1967–1970 war between Israel and Egypt. Following the 1967 Six-Day War, no serious diplomatic efforts were made to resolve the issues at the heart of the Arab–Israeli conflict.
Born to mixed English-American parentage, this statesman led his nation through its darkest hour as Prime Minister during World War II. Who?
Winston Churchill: British statesman and writer (1874–1965)
He ran the KGB for 15 years before briefly becoming the Soviet Union's General Secretary in 1982 — and decades earlier, as ambassador to Hungary, helped crush its 1956 uprising. Who is he?
Yuri Andropov: Leader of the Soviet Union from 1982 to 1984.

Which of these four began earliest?
Messerschmitt Bf 109 (founded 1937) is the earliest of the four.
Perl (founded 1987) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Alessandro Volta is a physicist. Throughout his life, Volta enjoyed a certain amount of closeness with the emperor who conferred upon him numerous honours.
Which one below is best known as a chemist?
Wallace Carothers is a chemist. Carothers was a group leader at the DuPont Experimental Station laboratory, near Wilmington, Delaware, where most polymer research was done.
What is the atomic number of Carbon?
Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
In what year was Bernard Arnault born?
Bernard Arnault: Bernard Jean Étienne Arnault (born 5 March 1949) is a French businessman.
In what year was Radon discovered?
Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.
In what year was Adenosine triphosphate discovered?
Adenosine triphosphate: When consumed in a metabolic process, ATP converts either to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) or to adenosine monophosphate (AMP).
Mil Mi-26: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. The Mil Mi-26 (Russian: Миль Ми-26, NATO reporting name: Halo) is a Soviet/Russian heavy transport helicopter.
Which country is Artemy Lebedev from?
Artemy Lebedev: Russia. Artemy Andreyevich Lebedev (Russian: Артемий Андреевич Лебедев; born 13 February 1975) is a Russian designer, entrepreneur and Internet personality.
Who is credited with discovering Rhodium?
Rhodium: William Hyde Wollaston. Rhodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rh and atomic number 45.
Who is credited with discovering Ibuprofen?
Ibuprofen: Stewart Adams. Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.
Who is credited with discovering Carbon?
Carbon: Antoine Lavoisier. Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
Drugs that meddle with this neurotransmitter can do everything from paralyze to cause convulsions, since it's the signal motor neurons use to activate muscles. What is it?
Acetylcholine (ACh) is an organic compound that functions in the brain and body of many types of animals (including humans) as a neurotransmitter.
Believed to be an autoimmune attack that breaches the immune privilege of hair follicles, this condition typically leaves a few coin-sized bald spots on the scalp — what is it?
Alopecia areata (AA), also known as spot baldness, is a condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body.
This British-American theoretical physicist at the University of Illinois reshaped our understanding of superfluid helium, work crowned by the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics — who was he?
Anthony Leggett (26 March 1938 - 8 March 2026) was a British-American theoretical physicist and professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC).
First described in 1740, this flowering-plant family rivals only the orchid family in sheer number of species, with over 32,000 recognized today — what family is it?
Asteraceae is a large family of flowering plants that consists of over 32,000 known species in over 1,900 genera within the order Asterales.
Once chairman of the Nasdaq, this financier admitted to masterminding the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, estimated at $65 billion — who was he?

Bernie Madoff (April 29, 1938 - April 14, 2021) was an American financier, con artist, and stock broker who was the admitted mastermind of the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, worth an estimated $65 billion.
Caused by a toxin that thrives in low-oxygen conditions — the same one sold cosmetically as 'botox' — this rare illness brings blurred vision and creeping paralysis but rarely a fever. What is it?
Botulism is a rare and potentially fatal illness caused by botulinum toxin (commonly referred to as botox), which is produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum.

First synthesized in 1950 by bombarding curium with helium-4 ions, this synthetic actinide element carries atomic number 98, symbol Cf, and the second-highest atomic mass of any element — which element?
Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.

Appearing in early childhood with symptoms like poor coordination and stiff or weak muscles, this group of movement disorders does not worsen over time even though symptoms become more noticeable in a child's first years — which condition?
Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of movement disorders that appear in early childhood.
In 2023, she became the first woman ever to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on her own, honored for her research on women in the labor market — who is this Harvard economist?
Claudia Goldin (born May 14, 1946) is an American economic historian and labor economist.
This fungal plant disease disfigures maize with galls, yet in Mexican cuisine the infected kernels are prized as huitlacoche, a filling for quesadillas and soups — which disease?
Corn smut is a plant disease caused by the pathogenic fungus Mycosarcoma maydis, synonym Ustilago maydis.
Nicknamed for the material that made up most of its airframe, this British twin-engined combat aircraft of World War II was one of the fastest operational planes of 1941. What aircraft is this?
De Havilland Mosquito was a British twin-engined, multi-role combat aircraft, introduced during the Second World War.
This C-shaped first section of the small intestine connects the stomach to the jejunum and is the body's principal site for absorbing iron — what is it?
Duodenum is the first section of the small intestine in most vertebrates, including mammals, reptiles, and birds.

It's the creation of economic value by spotting and commercializing opportunities — a venture that demands serious initiative and shoulders real risk. What is this process, named from a French word for the risk-taker who runs it?

Entrepreneurship is the creation or extraction of economic value by identifying and commercializing opportunities to deliver products or services, a process that typically requires considerable initiation and bears risk.

This synthetic opioid is 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine and is now notorious in emergency medicine. Initially developed as a pain medication for cancer patients and post-surgical recovery, it works by activating opioid receptors — what is this drug?
Fentanyl is a highly potent synthetic opioid of the piperidine family, used primarily as pain medication.
Home to the supermassive black hole known as Sagittarius A*, this point roughly 26,000 light-years from Earth marks the barycenter around which the Milky Way rotates — what is it?
Galactic Center is the barycenter of the Milky Way and a corresponding point on the rotational axis of the galaxy.
This week-long 2010 manhunt across Tyne and Wear and Northumberland ended when the fugitive shot himself following a six-hour standoff near Rothbury. What event is it?
Goose (pl.: geese) is a bird of any of several waterfowl species in the family Anatidae.
This usually benign tumor made of blood vessels typically appears on a baby's skin at birth or within weeks, often on the face, scalp, chest, or back, then shrinks over childhood — what is it?
Hemangioma is a usually benign vascular tumor derived from blood vessel cell types.
Sold as a 3 percent solution for the bathroom cabinet but explosive when concentrated, this oxidizer and antiseptic carries the formula H2O2 — what is it?
Hydrogen peroxide is a chemical compound with the formula H2O2.
This flowering plant genus boasts 310 species with showy blooms, some known by the common name 'flags' and a horticultural subgroup called 'junos' — what genus is it?
Iris (plant) is a flowering plant genus of 310 accepted species with showy flowers.
Two years after unveiling the first mechanical television system, this Scottish engineer achieved the first-ever transatlantic television transmission in 1928 — who is he?
John Logie Baird (13 August 1888 - 14 June 1946) was a Scottish inventor, electrical engineer and innovator who demonstrated the world's first mechanical television system on 26 January 1926.
Native to southern China but long cultivated in Japan and Southeast Asia, this small fruit closely resembles an orange in color and texture but is only about the size of a large olive — what is it?
Kumquat are a group of small, angiosperm, fruit-bearing trees in the family Rutaceae.
One of only five people to win multiple Nobel Prizes, this American chemist and peace activist is the sole person to have received two unshared Nobels — one in Chemistry, one for Peace. Who is he?
Linus Pauling (February 28, 1901 - August 19, 1994) was an American chemist and peace activist.

This colorless, highly water-soluble inorganic salt forms hydrates holding up to 12 water molecules per unit, and its anhydrous form is industry's main source for producing a lightweight, silvery-white structural metal — which compound is it?
Magnesium chloride is an inorganic compound with the formula MgCl2.
First made in 1955 by bombarding einsteinium with alpha particles, this synthetic element 101 is named for the father of the periodic table — what is it?
Mendelevium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Md (formerly Mv) and atomic number 101.
These cylindrical, burrowing insects have small eyes and shovel-like front limbs highly adapted for digging underground — name the family?
Mole cricket are members of the insect family Gryllotalpidae, in the order Orthoptera (grasshoppers, locusts, and crickets).
In this category of over 80 recognized conditions, the body's adaptive immune system mistakenly attacks its own healthy tissue as though it were foreign. What is it?

Navel (clinically known as the umbilicus; pl.: umbilici or umbilicuses; also known as the belly button or tummy button) is a protruding, flat, or hollowed area on the abdomen at the attachment site of the umbilical cord.
First described by Linnaeus in 1758, this medium-sized spotted cat of the Americas is a skilled climber, leaper, and swimmer that hunts armadillos and opossums by night — which cat is it?
Ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) is a medium-sized spotted wild cat that reaches 40-50 cm (16-20 in) at the shoulders and weighs between 7 and 15.5 kg (15 and 34 lb) on average.
Contrasted with 'normophilic' interests and famously tallied at up to 549 types by Anil Aggrawal, this contested clinical category covers atypical sexual attraction — what's its name?
Paraphilia is an uncommon, intense, and persistent sexual arousal or attraction to anything not sexual by nature, though preference is favored for specific designations.
Members of the family Phasianidae and native to Eurasia, these game birds snack on insects and fresh green shoots come summer — what are they?
Pheasant are birds of several genera within the family Phasianidae in the order Galliformes.
Built from poetic devices like onomatopoeia, rhyme schemes, and rhythm, this literary art uses the musical qualities of language to suggest more than the words plainly say — what is it?

Poetry (from the Greek word poiesis, "making") is a form of literary art that uses aesthetic and often rhythmic qualities of language to evoke meanings in addition to, or in place of, literal or surface-level meanings.

Named early in the history of microbiology for its widespread presence in water and plant seeds, which genus of gram-negative bacteria includes an opportunistic human pathogen infamous in hospitals as well as plant and soil-dwelling species?
Pseudomonas is a genus of gram-negative bacteria belonging to the family Pseudomonadaceae in the class Gammaproteobacteria.
What fat-soluble alcohol form of vitamin A — found in fish, dairy, and meat — is essential for vision, skin maintenance, and immune function, and is used as a supplement to prevent xerophthalmia?
Retinol is a hydrolytic metabolite of retinyl esters belonging to the group of vitamin A1 as an alcohol form.

These lizard-like amphibians, grouped in the order Urodela, keep a tail throughout both their larval and adult life stages — unlike their tailless amphibian cousins the frogs and toads. What animal is it?

Salamander are a group of amphibians typically characterized by their lizard-like appearance, with slender bodies, blunt snouts, short limbs projecting at right angles to the body, and the presence of a tail in both larvae and adults.

Essentially plasma with the clotting factors and cells removed, this pale yellow fluid still carries antibodies, hormones, and electrolytes and is central to typing tests done before a transfusion — what is it?
Serum (blood) is the fluid and solvent component of blood which does not play a role in clotting.
Native to a swath from Ireland to southern China, this aromatic herb is used to flavor food and herbal teas, and its extracted oil serves as both a flavoring and a scent — what is it?

Spearmint (Mentha spicata), also known as garden mint, common mint, lamb mint and mackerel mint, is native to Europe and southern temperate Asia, extending from Ireland in the west to southern China in the east.
This Chinese physician and revolutionary led the 1911 Revolution, overthrew the Qing dynasty, and founded the Republic of China as its first president. Who was he?
Sun Yat-sen (12 November 1866 - 12 March 1925) was a Chinese physician, revolutionary and political philosopher who founded the Republic of China (ROC) and the Kuomintang (KMT).

Proposed by Albert Einstein in special and general forms published in 1905 and 1915, this framework superseded 200-year-old Newtonian mechanics and explains gravitation's relation to the other forces of nature — name it?
Theory of relativity comprises two physics theories by Albert Einstein: special relativity and general relativity. Special relativity applies to all physical phenomena in the absence of gravity.

Picture a spider that never learned to spin: these extinct arachnids lacked silk-producing spinnerets and wore an abdomen split into three or five distinct plates. Which order, known from the Silurian to the Permian?
Trigonotarbida is a group of extinct arachnids whose fossil record extends from the late Silurian to the early Permian (Pridoli to Sakmarian).
Its wild form is dioecious while domesticated versions bear hermaphrodite flowers — this Mediterranean-native plant is the ancestor of nearly all wine and table varieties — what species?

Vitis vinifera is a species of flowering plant, native to the Mediterranean region, Central Europe, and southwestern Asia, from Morocco and Portugal north to southern Germany and east to northern Iran.
Native from Panama to southern Canada, this plant genus of 50 species belongs to the asparagus family alongside the agaves — name the genus?
Yucca (YUK-) is both the scientific name and common name for a genus native to North America from Panama to southern Canada.
This protrusion in the neck, formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage around the larynx, becomes more prominent in most men during puberty — what is it?
Adam's apple: Feature of the neck. The Adam's apple is the protrusion in the neck formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage surrounding the larynx, typically visible in men and less so in women.

This organic functional group, structured R−CH=O and alternatively called a formyl group when isolated from its side chain, appears throughout biologically and technologically important chemicals — what is it?
Aldehyde: Organic compound containing the functional group R–CH=O.

Once sold as Elavil, this tricyclic antidepressant is now often a second-line choice — used as much for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and migraines as for depression, thanks to its many side effects. Which drug?
Amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant. Due to the frequency and prominence of side effects, amitriptyline is generally considered a second-line therapy for these indications.
This British-American theoretical physicist at the University of Illinois won the 2003 Nobel Prize for pioneering work on superfluidity and the quantum physics of low-temperature helium — who was he?
Known as mugwort or wormwood, this daisy-family plant has long been used for both medicinal and culinary purposes — what species is it?

Artemisia vulgaris: Medicinal plant known as common mugwort. It is one of several species in the genus Artemisia commonly known as mugwort, although Artemisia vulgaris is the species most often called mugwort.
Blooming for weeks each spring and thriving in the shade under trees, these flowering shrubs belong to the genus Rhododendron — what are they called?
Azalea: Subgroup of rhododendron flowering shrubs.
Commonly known as barberry, this genus of deciduous and evergreen shrubs grows worldwide except Australia, and one of its species is Oregon's official state flower — what genus is it?
Berberis: Genus of flowering plants representing the barberry family.
This North American wild cat earns its name from the black-tipped, stubby tail it sports, along with distinctive black bars on its forelegs — one of the four species of lynx. Which animal is it?
Bobcat: Medium-sized North American wild cat.

After resigning from Evergreen State College following 2017 protests over campus racial equity, this podcaster and former evolutionary biology professor was named part of the 'intellectual dark web' — who is he?
Bret Weinstein: American podcaster and author (born 1969)
Formed when quicklime reacts with water, this compound goes by names like slaked lime and builders' lime, and is used in food prep under the additive code E526 — what is it?
Calcium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Ca(OH)2.

This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' for reactions that work inside living systems, building chemical tools to study the cell-surface sugars called glycans. Who is she?
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like herb is brewed into calming teas and can trigger uterine contractions in its Roman variety — what is it?
Chamomile: Common name for several daisy-like plants.
In this chronic liver condition, healthy tissue is replaced by scar tissue and regenerative nodules, choking blood flow and causing portal hypertension — what is it called?
Cirrhosis: Chronic disease of the liver, characterized by fibrosis.
In mathematics, this is a selection of items from a set where the order of choosing them does not matter, unlike a permutation — what is it called?

Combination: Selection of items from a set. In mathematics, a combination is a selection of items from a set that has distinct members, such that the order of selection does not matter (unlike permutations).

First published in 1785 by a French physicist, this principle holds that the electrostatic force between two charged particles is proportional to their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them — which principle is it?
Coulomb's law: Fundamental physical law of electromagnetism.

Originally bred for the hunt and later famous for trotting alongside horse-drawn firehouse carriages, this white breed with dark spots traces its roots to a region on the Adriatic coast — which breed?
Dalmatian dog: Croatian hunting/carriage/coach dog breed.
Approved for medical use in the US back in 1950, this medication treats intestinal spasms such as those seen in irritable bowel syndrome — what is it called?
This first section of the small intestine, often the principal site of iron absorption, connects the stomach to the middle portion of the intestine — what is it?
Duodenum: First section of the small intestine. The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine in most vertebrates, including mammals, reptiles, and birds.
This German chess player, mathematician and philosopher held the world title for 27 years — the longest reign ever — partly by a famously "psychological" approach to rattling opponents; who was he?

This branch of zoology studying animal behavior traces its scientific roots to Darwin and came into its own in the 1930s through Nobel laureates Tinbergen, Lorenz, and von Frisch — what's the field called?
Sold under the brand name Pepcid, this H2-receptor-blocking medication treats stomach-acid conditions like peptic ulcers and begins working within an hour — which drug?
Famotidine: Medication that reduces stomach acid.
Also nicknamed 'muscae volitantes' — Latin for flying flies — these tiny shadowy specks drift across your vision, especially noticeable against a blank blue sky. What are they?
Floater: Deposits within the eye's vitreous humour.
Named in 1753 from Greek words for 'milk' and 'flower,' this genus of about 20 bulbous perennial species is better known by its common name, snowdrop — what is its scientific genus?
Galanthus: Genus of flowering plants in the family Amaryllidacee.

Likely first domesticated by Austronesian peoples in Maritime Southeast Asia, this herbaceous perennial is grown for the spicy rhizome that puts it in the same family as turmeric and cardamom — what is it?
Ginger: Species of plant used as a spice.
Also known as the Congo variety, this African bird in the family Psittacidae lost its old 'African' nickname once a related Timneh species was split off as its own species — what is it?
Grown as deciduous shrubs across the temperate Northern Hemisphere and related to the birch family, this plant produces a popular round brown nut — which plant genus?
Discovered in 1910 and stored in mast cells and basophils, this compound triggers immune responses and doubles as a neurotransmitter in the brain, spinal cord, and uterus — what is it?
Histamine: Organic compound involved in immune responses.
This nearly worldwide genus of flowering plants — commonly called St. John's wort — was the subject of a definitive taxonomic monograph identifying 36 sections within it. Which genus?
Hypericum: Genus of flowering plants known as St. John's worts.
This Belgian-American physicist-mathematician is best known for wavelets that revolutionized image compression — a family of them even bears her name; who is she?
Ingrid Daubechies: Belgian physicist and mathematician (born 1954)
Sometimes called the founder of pneumatic chemistry, this 17th-century Brussels physician coined the word 'gas' and ran a famous five-year willow-tree experiment. Who was he?
Jan Baptist van Helmont: Chemist and physician (1580–1644)
Fluent in Quechua after being raised in two Indigenous households as a child, this Peruvian novelist and anthropologist became known for his intimate portrayals of Andean culture — who is he?
Endemic to a handful of Indonesian islands, this apex predator is the largest living lizard — males reaching 3 metres and 150 kg — and hunts in groups, a rarity among reptiles. What is it?
Komodo dragon: Largest living species of lizard. The largest extant population lives within the Komodo National Park in Eastern Indonesia.
Also known as Peruvian ginseng, this Andean root crop is grown at high altitude in Peru and Bolivia and exported worldwide as a dietary powder — what plant is it?
Lepidium meyenii: Plant species native to South America.
This American WWII twin-engine, twin-boom fighter carried its pilot alone in a central nacelle and served as fighter-bomber, night fighter, and long-range escort — which aircraft was it?
Lockheed P-38 Lightning: American twin-engined fighter of WWII. The Lockheed P-38 Lightning is an American single-seat, twin-engined fighter aircraft that was used during World War II.
Occurring naturally as the mineral brucite, this poorly soluble white solid neutralizes stomach acid in a well-known antacid — which compound?
Magnesium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Mg(OH)2.
Among the first women in Canada to earn a medical doctorate, this physician-chemist is best known for her 1913 work with Leonor Michaelis on enzyme kinetics — who was she?
Maud Menten: Canadian physician and chemist (1879–1960)
Marketed under brand names like Quaalude and Sopor, this sedative was pulled from commercial production in the mid-1980s due to widespread misuse — which drug?
Most under a millimeter long, these eight-legged arachnids include the parasite that plagues honeybee colonies and the species behind scabies in humans — what are they?
This semiaquatic rodent swims using webbed hind feet while its scaly, flattened tail works mainly as a rudder for steering — what is it?
Muskrat: Species of rodent. The muskrat or common muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus) is a medium-sized semiaquatic rodent.
This group of three genetic conditions causes nervous-system tumors; its first type brings café au lait skin spots and scoliosis, while its second causes early hearing loss — what's it called?
Neurofibromatosis: Three genetic disorders involving benign tumors of the nervous system.
This condition of involuntary eye movement can be triggered by stimulating the ear's semicircular canals — for example with the caloric test — while the head stays still. What is it?
Nystagmus: Dysfunction of eye movement. Nystagmus is a condition of involuntary (or voluntary, in some cases) eye movement.
This surgical medical subspecialty treats the ear, nose, and throat — organs connected via the Eustachian tube — earning its specialists the nickname 'ENT surgeons.' What field is it?
Otorhinolaryngology: Medical specialty of the head and neck.
From the Greek for 'the study of disease,' this medical field diagnoses illness largely by analyzing tissue and cell samples — what is it?
Pathology: Study of disease. The word pathology also refers to the study of disease in general, incorporating a wide range of biology research fields and medical practices.
Native to Eurasia but now introduced worldwide, this game bird has been flagged in the UK as a threat to endangered native adders — what is it?

Commonly known as plantains or fleaworts — though unrelated to the banana-like cooking fruit of the same name — this genus of roughly 200 mostly herbaceous flowering plants tops out around 24 inches tall. Which genus?
Plantago: Genus of flowering plants. Plantago is a genus of about 200 species of flowering plants in the family Plantaginaceae, commonly called plantains or fleaworts.
This glucocorticoid medication used to suppress the immune system is actually a prodrug that the liver must convert into its active form before it works — what is it?
Prednisone: Steroid medication. It is also used to treat high blood calcium due to cancer and adrenal insufficiency along with other corticosteroids.
Emitting beams of radiation from its magnetic poles like a cosmic lighthouse, this highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star produces remarkably precise, repeating pulses — what is it?
Pulsar: Type of neutron star with beams of radiation.

A canine native to the southeastern United States, intermediate in size between the coyote and gray wolf. For a century its status as a separate species has been debated — some call it a coywolf. Name this animal.
Red wolf: Canid native to the southeastern United States. Fish and Wildlife Service recognizes the red wolf as an endangered species and grants it protected status.
A Jesuit priest and polymath from the Republic of Ragusa produced an early precursor of atomic theory and, in 1753, discovered that the Moon has no atmosphere — who was he?
Roger Joseph Boscovich: Croat-Italian physicist and writer (1711–1787)
This Taiwanese-American physicist shared the 1976 Nobel Prize with Burton Richter for discovering the subatomic J/ψ particle. Who is he?
Samuel C. C. Ting: Nobel prize winning physicist.
Native to the western slopes of California's Sierra Nevada, this endangered conifer is the largest tree species on Earth, with a record height of 94.8 meters — what is it?
Sequoiadendron giganteum: Species of tree native to North America.

Named in 1842 from Brazilian fossils and often called a saber-toothed tiger despite no close kinship to true tigers, this genus of prehistoric predator roamed the Americas until the early Holocene — which animal?
Smilodon: Extinct genus of saber-toothed cat.
With eight arms plus two extra tentacles for grabbing prey, this soft-bodied mollusc has an internal chitin rod called a gladius instead of a true skeleton — what creature is it?

A retired US Navy captain, this NASA astronaut became the first woman to fly on an orbital spacecraft's test flight in 2024 and had her ISS stay extended by more than nine months due to technical issues — who is she?
Sunita Williams: U.S. Navy officer and NASA astronaut (born 1965)
A math prodigy who abandoned academia in 1969 for a reclusive cabin life, the 'Unabomber' mailed bombs for 17 years and published a 35,000-word anti-technology manifesto — who was he?
Shaped like a butterfly and sitting in the neck just below the Adam's apple, this endocrine gland secretes hormones that regulate metabolic rate — which gland is it?
Thyroid: Endocrine gland in the neck. The lower two thirds of the lobes are connected by a thin band of tissue called the isthmus (pl.: isthmi).
Also known as tic douloureux, this chronic pain disorder causes sudden, shock-like facial pain and has been linked to depression — what condition is it?
Trigeminal neuralgia: Neurological pain disorder. There are two main types: typical and atypical trigeminal neuralgia.
This condition causes involuntary muscle spasms that interfere with vaginal penetration, usually rooted in a fear that it will cause pain — what is it?
Vaginismus: Involuntary muscle spasm that interferes with vaginal penetration.
One of the oldest leaf vegetables eaten by humans, this aquatic member of the cabbage family shares its peppery bite with relatives like mustard, radish, and wasabi — what is it?
Watercress: Species of flowering plant in the cabbage family.
Spread mainly by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, this viral illness can cause a brief recovery before a relapse brings liver damage and jaundice — what disease is it?
Yellow fever: Viral disease. In most cases, symptoms include fever, chills, loss of appetite, nausea, muscle pains—particularly in the back—and headaches.
Gadolinium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for gadolinium is Gd. Gadolinium is a chemical element; it has symbol Gd and atomic number 64.
The symbol for chromium is Cr. Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.

In what year was Alan Rickman born?
Alan Rickman: Alan Sidney Patrick Rickman (21 February 1946 – 14 January 2016) was an English actor.
In what year was Michelle Williams born?
Michelle Williams (actress): Michelle Ingrid Williams (born September 9, 1980) is an American actress.
In what year was Christopher Reeve born?
Christopher Reeve: Christopher D'Olier Reeve (September 25, 1952 – October 10, 2004) was an American actor, activist, director, and author.
In what year was Vincent Cassel born?
Vincent Cassel (French: [vɛ̃sɑ̃ kasɛl]; né Crochon [kʁɔʃɔ̃]; born 23 November 1966) is a French actor.
In what year was Zoë Kravitz born?
Zoë Kravitz: Zoë Isabella Kravitz (born December 1, 1988) is an American actress, singer, and filmmaker.
In what year was Lizzy Caplan born?
Lizzy Caplan: Elizabeth Anne Caplan (born June 30, 1982) is an American actress.
In what year was Russell Brand born?
Russell Brand: Russell Edward Brand (born 4 June 1975) is an English comedian, actor, podcaster, and media personality.

Kit Harington: Christopher Catesby Harington (born 26 December 1986), known professionally as Kit Harington, is an English actor.

Eddie Murphy: Edward Regan Murphy (born April 3, 1961) is an American comedian, actor, and singer.

Cole Hauser: Cole Kenneth Hauser (born March 22, 1975) is an American actor.
In what year was Julianne Moore born?
